title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a clerk's account book fills up with songs to Kali

segments.voice: Yesterday, a conch at dusk for the Goddess, and a drum in the next lane for Krishna: two streams, not walls.

An office in Calcutta. A young clerk is supposed to be copying figures into the account book, rows of numbers, day after day. But the other clerks notice the margins of his ledger filling up with something else: lines of verse, songs to Kali, the dark Mother. Somebody takes the book to the employer, expecting the young man to be fired. The employer opens it, starts reading, and doesn't stop. Today, the Shakta stream through one singer: Ramprasad Sen.
screen: `A CLERK AND HIS LEDGER.` → `SONGS IN THE MARGINS.` → `THE EMPLOYER READS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the employer was so moved that instead of dismissing him, he sent Ramprasad home to his village with an allowance, so he could do nothing but sing. His songs, the stories say, spread from village to village, sung by boatmen and farmers, and tradition gives a melody his name. Listen to how he talks to Kali. Not like a courtier bowing to a queen. Like a child to his mother. In one song, in paraphrase, he complains: other children have a mother who looks after them, so why am I left like this? Is this how a mother behaves? He sulks, he pleads, he threatens to tell everyone. That's the Shakta stream at its warmest. The Goddess may be fierce, with a sword and a necklace of heads, but to the singer she is Ma, and a child is allowed to be cross with his mother. People tell a story about him. He was mending a fence and needed someone to hold the rope on the other side. His young daughter came and held it. Later, when he thanked her, she said she'd been away the whole time. So who held the rope? In the story, the Mother herself, wearing a little girl's face. And his songs aren't only sweet. In one, he scolds his own mind as a lazy farmer: this human life is a good field, and you've left it lying fallow. Tend it, and gold would grow. Tender with the Mother, hard on himself. That's the voice that came out of an account book.
screen: `SONGS IN THE ACCOUNT BOOK` · `A CHILD, CROSS WITH HIS MOTHER` · `WHO HELD THE ROPE?` · `THE FIELD LEFT FALLOW`

segments.voice: Picture your day as a small plot of ground: some of it planted, things you tended and people you looked after, and some lying fallow, a thing you keep meaning to start, a call you haven't made. Walk around the field in your mind and notice, without scolding yourself. If you pray, you can call on the Mother, or on God, as the one who holds the rope on the other side.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams: the Shakta stream in Ramprasad Sen, the clerk who filled his ledger with songs and talked to Kali like a child to his mother. Today's word.

howItsDone: Ramprasad's songs to Kali are sung in Bengal at Kali Puja, at home and in devotional gatherings, as part of the song tradition known as Shyama Sangeet.

notes: Editor pass: the fence story's garbled sentence ('when he went inside, his daughter said...') rewritten; 'a melody even took his name' softened to 'tradition gives a melody his name'.
The ledger story (employer often named as Durgacharan Mitra) and the allowance (in some tellings from Raja Krishnachandra of Nadia) are told as tradition; confirm the paraphrase.
The fence story: tradition says Kali, in the form of his daughter, helped him bind the fence. Confirm the version told (daughter absent; the Mother held the rope).

Song paraphrases: the complaint to the Mother (a child neglected), and 'mana tumi krishi kaj jano na' (O mind, you don't know how to farm; the field of human birth lies fallow; tend it and gold would grow). Confirm.
'Ramprasadi sur' as a named melody: confirm.
Kali's necklace of heads is mentioned only as iconography; confirm tone is respectful for Shakta listeners.
